noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that plants respond to stimuli
describe the geotropic and phototropic responses of roots and stems
understand the role of auxin in the phototropic response of stems

primer.text: You know plants need light for photosynthesis and water from the soil. This note explains how rooted organisms still manage to steer themselves: shoots grow toward light and away from gravity, roots do the opposite, and a chemical called auxin runs the whole steering system. Learn the tropism vocabulary here — it is heavily examined.

lessons.title: Tropisms: directional growth toward and away
lessons.opening: Plants cannot walk away from problems, so they grow their way out instead. Directional growth toward or away from light and gravity is called a tropism: shoots climb toward light and against gravity, while roots push downward with gravity and away from light, anchoring the plant and reaching water.
keyPoints: Plants grow in response to stimuli such as light and gravity.
Directional growth responses to light and gravity are named tropisms.
Growth toward the stimulus is positive; growth away is negative.
Shoots show positive phototropism and negative geotropism.
Roots show positive geotropism and negative phototropism.

low.restatement: Shoots bend toward light and upward against gravity; roots drive downward with gravity and away from light.
low.analogy: A plant is a two-way traveller — its top chases sunshine while its bottom hunts deep water.
low.examPointer: Learn the four pairings in the table: shoot or root, with light or gravity, each carrying its sign.

medium.restatement: Tropisms couple a directional stimulus to growth direction: phototropism orients shoots for photosynthesis while geotropism anchors roots and aims them at soil water and minerals.
medium.analogy: Think of a hotel with two concierges — one steers guests toward the bright lobby, the other toward the underground car park.
medium.examPointer: Definitions earn marks: name the tropism, the organ and the sign — 'positive phototropism of shoots' is a complete answer.

options.text: A directional growth response toward or away from a stimulus
options.explanation: Tropisms are directional growth responses of plants.

options.text: A rapid movement of a whole plant
options.explanation: Plants respond by growth, not by moving their position.
Chemicals called auxins cause tropisms but are not tropisms themselves.
The named tropisms answer light and gravity.

check.stem: How do shoots respond to light?

options.text: Positive phototropism — growth toward the light
options.explanation: Shoots grow toward light to catch sunlight for leaves.

options.text: Negative phototropism — growth away from light
options.explanation: That describes roots' light response.
That is the roots' gravity response.
Phototropism is a core plant response.

check.stem: How do roots respond to gravity?

options.text: Positive geotropism — growth toward gravity, into the soil
options.explanation: Roots grow downward with gravity to anchor and absorb water.

options.text: Negative geotropism — growth away from gravity
options.explanation: That is the shoots' gravity response.
Phototropism answers light, not gravity.
Root growth is directional, not random.

check.stem: Which pairing describes roots' response to light correctly?

options.explanation: Roots grow away from light.

options.text: Negative phototropism — growth away from the light source
options.explanation: Roots grow downward into soil, away from light.
The table assigns roots a negative phototropic response.

options.text: Roots bend toward light to photosynthesise
options.explanation: Photosynthesis is the shoots' job.

check.stem: Why do roots grow downward into the soil?

options.explanation: Light is the shoots' target.

options.text: To hold the plant firm and draw up soil water plus dissolved minerals
options.explanation: Those are the stated reasons for downward root growth.
Predator escape is not the named reason.
Reproduction is unrelated to root direction.

check.modelAnswer: A plant's directional growth response to gravity, toward it (positive, as in roots) or away (negative, as in shoots).

check.stem: State the two tropism signs a shoot displays.
check.modelAnswer: Positive phototropism toward light and negative geotropism away from gravity.

check.stem: Explain why a shoot's positive phototropic response helps the plant survive.
check.modelAnswer: Growing toward light positions the leaves where they can absorb the most sunlight for photosynthesis, so the plant makes more food, grows stronger and outcompetes shaded neighbours — the tropism converts a stimulus directly into a survival advantage.

check.stem: A seedling germinates on a dark windowsill with light coming from one side only. Describe its expected growth pattern.
check.modelAnswer: The shoot curves toward the window (positive phototropism) while growing upward against gravity (negative geotropism); the root grows away from the light and downward into the compost with gravity (positive geotropism, negative phototropism).

lessons.title: Auxin: the chemistry of the phototropic bend
sourceHeadings: The Role of Auxin in Phototropism
lessons.opening: Auxin is the plant's growth coordinator. Made in the shoot tips, it moves just behind the tip where it makes existing cells elongate; the more auxin, the faster the stretch. When light strikes one side, auxin collects on the shaded side, those cells lengthen faster, and the shoot bends toward the light.
keyPoints: Auxins are plant growth regulators coordinating directional growth.
Auxin is manufactured in shoot tips and moves downward to the zone just behind, where cell division happens.
Auxin makes existing cells elongate; higher auxin means faster elongation.
Even light gives an even auxin spread, so shoots grow straight.
One-sided light concentrates auxin on the shaded side, whose cells lengthen faster and bend the shoot toward the light.

low.restatement: Tip-made auxin pools on the shaded side, stretching those cells faster, so the shoot curves sunward.
low.analogy: Like a rowing boat turning — the shaded-side cells are the rowers pulling harder on one side.
low.examPointer: Say cell elongation, never cell division — the exam hint penalises answers claiming new cells appear.

medium.restatement: Auxin's gradient across the shoot is the mechanism: uniform light gives uniform elongation, unilateral light gives an elongation gap that bends the organ.
medium.analogy: A bimetallic strip bends because one metal expands more; a shoot bends because one side elongates more.
medium.examPointer: Quote the dose relationship — the more auxin, the faster the elongation — when explaining the bend.

options.text: In the tips of growing shoots
options.explanation: Auxin is mostly made in the shoot tips.
Root hairs absorb water; they do not make auxin here.
Flowers handle reproduction in this note's scope.
Production is tied to shoot tips, not leaves or darkness.

check.stem: What does auxin do to cells behind the tip?

options.explanation: Auxin makes existing cells get longer; more auxin means faster elongation.

options.text: Causes them to divide into many new cells
options.explanation: The exam hint is explicit — auxin elongates existing cells, it does not multiply them.

options.text: Kills them to shorten the shoot
options.explanation: Auxin promotes growth, not death.
No such transformation is described.

check.stem: Under one-sided light, where does auxin accumulate?

options.text: On the shaded side of the shoot
options.explanation: Auxin concentrates on the side away from the light.
That would bend the shoot away from light — the opposite of what happens.
Even spreading happens under all-round light, not one-sided light.

options.text: It drains out of the roots
options.explanation: Auxin stays within the shoot's growing region.

check.stem: What is the result of the shaded side elongating faster?

options.text: The shoot bends and grows in the direction of the light
options.explanation: Faster shaded-side growth curves the shoot sunward.

options.text: The shoot bends away from the light
options.explanation: That would need the sunlit side to elongate faster.
Growth bending, not breaking, occurs.
Growth continues — unevenly.

check.stem: Which statement about auxin and cell number is correct?

options.text: Auxin increases the number of cells in the shoot
options.explanation: This is precisely the trap — auxin does not increase cell number.

options.text: Auxin makes the cells that already exist get longer
options.explanation: Elongation of existing cells is the correct mechanism.
No cell removal is involved.

options.text: Cell number changes only in roots
options.explanation: The note concerns shoot elongation; cell number is unchanged.

check.stem: State where auxin is made and where it acts.
check.modelAnswer: Made in the shoot tips; it diffuses just behind the tip into the elongation zone.

check.stem: Give the dose relationship between auxin and elongation.
check.modelAnswer: The more auxin present, the faster the cells elongate and grow.

check.stem: Explain why writing 'the shoot grows toward the light because cells divide' loses marks.
check.modelAnswer: Because division implies new cells are being made, which is wrong: auxin causes the cells that already exist behind the tip to elongate, so the shoot bends by existing cells getting longer — claiming division shows the mechanism has been misidentified.

check.stem: A potted plant sits in a room whose only window is to its left. Using auxin, explain the shape it develops after two weeks.
check.modelAnswer: Light from the left makes auxin accumulate on the right (shaded) side of the shoot; those cells elongate faster than the lit side, so the stem curves leftward toward the window — a visible positive phototropic bend.

glossary.definition: A directional growth response of a plant toward (positive) or away (negative) from a stimulus such as light or gravity.
The directional growth response to light; positive in shoots, negative in roots.
The directional growth response to gravity; positive in roots, negative in shoots.
A plant growth regulator made in shoot tips that makes existing cells elongate faster where it accumulates.
